studies.Title: Consumption of Ultra-Processed Foods and Increased Risks of Prostate Cancer in a Random Sample of United States Adults.
studies.Reference: Consumption of Ultra-Processed Foods and Increased Risks of Prostate Cancer in a Random Sample of United States Adults.
studies.Population: Male adults in the United States National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey 2003-2023
studies.comparison_type: Combined second, third and fourth quartiles of ultra-processed food intake (% of total energy) versus lowest quartile

extraction_supporting_text.sample_size: Among 17,024 male adults, compared to those in the lowest, participants in the combined second, third, and fourth quartiles had a significant 29% higher risk of prostate cancer (p = 0.031), while those in the combined third and fourth quartiles had a significant 30% higher risk (p=0.035). Perhaps due to smaller sample sizes, those in the fourth quartile had a possible but non-significant increase of 31% (p=0.079).
extraction_supporting_text.effect_size: In adjusted analyses, corresponding values were 27% (p=0.045), 31% (p=0.037), and 34% (p=0.072). In these data, people with higher ultra-processed food intake had higher risks of prostate cancer.
extraction_supporting_text.confidence_interval: We used 90% confidence intervals to test for significance as harm was prespecified.
extraction_supporting_text.p_value: In adjusted analyses, corresponding values were 27% (p=0.045), 31% (p=0.037), and 34% (p=0.072).
extraction_supporting_text.comparison: compared to those in the lowest, participants in the combined second, third, and fourth quartiles had a significant 29% higher risk of prostate cancer
extraction_supporting_text.design: We used nationally representative data from the United States National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey from 2003 to 2023.
extraction_supporting_text.continent: a Random Sample of United States Adults
extraction_supporting_text.location: United States National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey
extraction_supporting_text.exposure_measurement: Ultra processed food intake was estimated from two 24-hour dietary recalls using the validated and widely used NOVA classification and categorized into quartiles based on the percentage of total energy intake.

headline.funnel_interpretation: Egger’s test is generally not recommended when fewer than 10 studies are available.
headline.results_interpretation: The pooled analysis of 2 studies yielded an effect size of 1.39 (95% CI: 0.58–3.31), indicating no statistically significant association between ultra-processed food intake and prostate cancer. Although the point estimate suggests a potential positive relationship, the confidence interval includes the null. These findings were accompanied by very high heterogeneity (I² = 86.82%), reflecting highly inconsistent results across studies.
